Tesla V14.3 self-driving review. The point releases will bring polish.

V15 will far exceed human levels of safety, even in completely unsupervised and complex situations.


Zack (@BLKMDL3)

600 miles in with FSD v14.3 already and here are my thoughts:

The improved reaction time is immediately noticeable and definitely quicker than a human could react. Yesterday a semi truck swerved fast into my lane and the car reacted insanely quickly to get me around them. Tesla says it’s 20% quicker but feels more than that- and it was already extremely good. 

I’ll start by saying FSD was already so great with v14.2 that it’s sometimes hard to find new things, but there some huge apparent changes immediately noticeable with v14.3. To those who think it’s not a big improvement over v14.2.x+, you’ll be very impressed and especially with some more polish. The reinforcement learning upgrades and thinking are noticeable. 

Parking is where you immediately notice some changes. In the release notes it says that parking is quicker and more decisive and it’s true. It has picked spots closer and quicker to the selected pin. My Y isn’t showing the new P pin graphic for parking pin for some reason, but it’s definitely parking closer than before with more thought to it. Looking forward to eventually getting more options to hopefully park either closer or further away from people.  

For the very first v14.3+ build, I have to say it’s pretty polished. The only gripe I have is the way it won’t get out of the left lane soon enough on highways. It likes to cruise in the left lane which isn’t ideal, it’s gotten better but the addition of reduction in unnecessary lane changes needs to be dialed back a bit. 

Lane changes are a huge plus with this build and they are quick, decisive and executed very well, smooth as butter too. Turn signals come on at way better times now in parking lots and at the perfect time on the road. 

I was lucky enough to get the update with 600 miles left of my 1800 mile Oregon road trip, so I pulled over to install it so I could get as much experience as possible with it to share with you all. So far 600+ miles in, I’m impressed. A few rough edges with the left lane behavior and the last few inches of parking are a bit slow 1/5 times until it puts it into park but with a point release update everything should be dialed in. The 350 mile drive home today from the Bay Area had zero intervention including all parking and charging. 

One thing I would love to see implemented is a reset button for the FSD stats page. Would be cool to have a specific trip meter for FSD stats on Trip A/B or make your own trip. I’ve been hinting at a pretty cool road trip next month with my 2025 Model 3 so it would be cool to have a reset for that.

Speed control seems good on highways, it’s matching traffic speed great. Braking is very impressive for sudden slowdowns, had a big one in San Jose last night it did a great job with from 80-10mph. 

HUGE improvements with stop sign behavior. The acceleration and deceleration are way smoother than before, much more pleasant. Mad Max takes off strong but again, a better curve than before. Mad Max is also polished a bit and feels great. FSD v14.3 did a great job in LA traffic once I got back and will go out this evening to film videos for everyone on my normal test loops. Let me know if there’s anything specific I should try or check out. 

Can’t wait to see how v14.3+ progresses especially with the upgraded reasoning coming to all scenarios soon. Some awesome additions here. 

THANK YOU everyone @Tesla_AI for all the hard work getting this update out. More videos to come.

Currently, I’d bet that FSD has already learned all the strategies for all scenarios, so all the “smart moves” you see on v14.3 will occasionally also be seen on v14.2 and earlier versions.

The issue is that the probability of the correct strategy is not always the highest, so it does not always get chosen. That means you cannot always reproduce those “highlight” moments.

An upgraded RL will mostly help re-sort those strategies so that better strategies have a higher chance of being chosen, resulting in more stable, predictable behavior. In other words, you’ll see those “highlights” more often with FSD v14.3.

I don’t have FSD 14.3, and I don’t think I’m in a hurry to get it. Maybe I’d like a slightly better parking upgrade, but honestly, for all the other problems 14.3 is supposed to solve, I have almost never run into them myself. Tesla is really trying to solve the last missing piece, and that piece is so tiny that I’m barely even aware of it. So I wonder whether it will actually just feel the same, as perfect as v14.2.2.5, and whether a lot of the perceived improvements people are sharing on X are probably just psychological suggestion. Why? Because at this point, without driving it for a year and collecting 10k miles, how can you be sure 14.3 is actually safer than 14.2?

Just finished my first drive on FSD 14.2.2.5, definitely an improvement but also noticed some weird behavior, such as swerving around tire marks. 

In fact, I’ve noticed that every recent FSD version that tries to improve pothole avoidance also seems more likely to unnecessarily swerve around tire marks.

I gave it some thought and realized that object avoidance, in general, is an extremely hard problem to solve. There are, in theory, unlimited types of road conditions, each requiring different strategies.

If you want to avoid everything, then what about leaves? You mostly want to ignore them. Do you still remember how FSD used to emergency brake for leaves?

However, if you want to run over them, then what about black ice? It is also dark, soft, and flat, but definitely needs to be avoided.

But then, if you choose to avoid those, what about tire marks? People still want FSD to ignore them, right?

To perfectly solve this problem, you would need near lossless compression of vision input, large model capacity to store general world knowledge, and lightning fast reasoning in order to react correctly.

Tesla Robotaxi: Mileage vs. At-fault crashes over time

Community notes are wrong, and many others are also wrong in speculating about my method. I’ll explain a few common misunderstandings here:

1. Lots of people assume that my analysis was calculated using fleet size, which is incorrect. The mileage data was extracted and projected using the Robotaxi mileage chart from the 2025 Q4 earnings report. So even if @ethanmckanna admitted that his website’s numbers are "misleading", that does not automatically make my analysis wrong.

2. I used the mileage from the 2025 Q4 earnings report, which reported 650K miles and is only about Austin. People incorrectly assume that includes both the SF Bay Area and Austin. However, as reported in Q3 2025, the SF Bay Area already had over 1 million miles back then. If the earnings report included SF Bay Area mileage, then it would have to be over 1 million miles at the end of Q4.

3. People pointed out that removing parking lot and stationary crashes is manipulating the data. I agree. However, I included a chart in the original post's replies to show how it looks when adding them back. As shown in that chart, the model can’t fit the data points, which means we don’t have enough data to make any conclusion if we include all kinds of crashes. I argue that removing those crashes was done transparently and only intended to make a limited prediction with higher confidence.


Raines (@raines1220)

I took a look at the Jan 2026 Robotaxi crash report, and the numbers are exciting🔥
- when safety passenger got removed (Jan 2026), MPI is ~200K miles. 
- Now (Feb 2026), MPI is ~400K miles. 
- I predict Robotaxi in Austin will fully surpass human drivers by the end of Q1 (before April).  

These numbers deviate from my last prediction due to several methodological improvements: 
- I previously underestimated Robotaxi mileage by ~2.5x because I was guessing mileage using a few data points and a fleet size chart. This is now corrected using the actual Robotaxi mileage chart reported in Tesla’s 2025 Q4 financial statement. 
- I realized parking lot dents and stationary crashes were adding significant noise. After removing them, the model fits the data much better.

I’ve been moving away from @cursor_ai because they’ve done a poor job with local parallel agents and are shipping more bugs than features.

As far as I know, many developers are moving away from Cursor for the same reasons, and I hope Cursor figure out a way to survive. After all, Cursor provided the best code review experience, in my opinion.

However, if they can’t survive, I hope they understand how critical it is to move fast and do proper testing at the same time.

Testing is easily 100x more important nowadays. I can have ~10 parallel agents filing PRs and another ~5 parallel agents reviewing them, with less and less human involvement in the loop. 

Without a proper testing solution, nothing will work. In other words, AI products will not work without solutions like @stably_ai. You must solve AI testing at the same time when you trying to solve AI coding.

I found another common misconception.

The Lemonade FSD discount does not specify the version, which means it includes HW3.

In fact, I don’t think Lemonade can tell which version you are using, so they basically conclude that 2x safer is the average (or worst) FSD can be, and they offer a 50% discount as a conservative starting point.

Based on my understanding, FSD (supervised) v14 is much better than 2x safer.

For those TSLAQ who blame Elon for overpromising, I want to share Parkinson’s Law:

“Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.”

I believe this is one of the fundamental principles behind how Elon tries to get things done.

In other words, if Elon promised that Tesla would achieve fully autonomous driving in 50 years, then most likely it would arrive in around 47 years.

But if you promise everyone it will happen next year and work insanely hard toward it, will it be achieved? Maybe. But one thing is certain: you will reach your maximum efficiency, and you will not delay (and likely will accelerate) the final success.
